manifest.description: Blueprint-compiled draft dispatch pack for math.nt.algebraic-number-theory (Phase 1 front-end; DRAFT only)

assets.title: Learning Objective
assets.content: The student defines an algebraic number field K=ℚ(α) as a finite extension of ℚ of degree [K:ℚ]=n; identifies the ring of integers O_K as the subring of algebraic integers in K; states that O_K is a Dedekind domain (Noetherian, integrally closed, every nonzero prime ideal is maximal); explains why O_K need not be a UFD and how ideal factorisation restores unique factorisation (every nonzero ideal factors uniquely into prime ideals); defines the ideal class group Cl(K)=I(O_K)/P(O_K) and its class number h_K; states Minkowski's bound; and explains the connection between the class number and Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes.

assets.title: ALL-RINGS-OF-INTEGERS-ARE-UFDS
assets.content: | MC-1 | ALL-RINGS-OF-INTEGERS-ARE-UFDS | Student assumes O_K is always a UFD, extending ℤ's unique factorisation; unaware that ℤ[√−5] (the ring of integers of ℚ(√−5)) fails UFD and this is the whole motivation for ideal theory | Type 5 — instruction-induced (ℤ is the canonical example of a number ring and it IS a UFD; students taught Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic as a universal truth apply it to all rings of integers without knowing the class number condition) |

assets.title: IDEAL-CLASS-GROUP-MEASURES-HOW-MANY-IDEALS-THERE-ARE
assets.content: | MC-2 | IDEAL-CLASS-GROUP-MEASURES-HOW-MANY-IDEALS-THERE-ARE | Student thinks h_K = |Cl(K)| counts total ideals or prime ideals of O_K; doesn't understand it measures failure of principal-ideal generation (i.e. failure of UFD property) | Type 3 — language contamination ("class" and "group" suggest a measure or collection of ideals per se; the actual meaning — equivalence classes of fractional ideals under principal-ideal equivalence — is abstract) |

assets.title: ALGEBRAIC-INTEGERS-IN-K-ARE-JUST-INTEGER-LINEAR-COMBINATIONS-OF-BASIS
assets.content: | MC-3 | ALGEBRAIC-INTEGERS-IN-K-ARE-JUST-INTEGER-LINEAR-COMBINATIONS-OF-BASIS | Student believes O_K = ℤ[α] always; doesn't know that O_K can be strictly larger than ℤ[α] for a generating element α | Type 5 — instruction-induced (examples like ℚ(√2) where O_K=ℤ[√2] and ℚ(√−1) where O_K=ℤ[i] confirm ℤ[α]=O_K; when the minimal polynomial has discriminant not equal to the field discriminant (e.g. ℚ(√5) where O_K=ℤ[(1+√5)/2]≠ℤ[√5]), students are caught off guard) |

assets.title: PARTIAL (doesn't understand ideal factorisation) → "An ideal I of O_K is a subgroup of O_K closed under multiplication by O_K. A prime ideal P is one where ab∈P implies a∈P or b∈P. In a Dedekind domain, every ideal (not just elements) factors uniquely into prime ideals. Example: in ℤ[√−5], the element 6 doesn't have unique factorisation, but the ideal (6) does: it equals a specific product of prime ideals, regardless of whether you start from 2×3 or (1+√−5)(1−√−5). assets.title: P91 Mastery Gate Sequence
assets.content:
**P77 — Problem Set (4 items):**
1. Determine the ring of integers O_K for K=ℚ(√−3), ℚ(√6), and ℚ(√13). Compute the discriminant of each.
2. In ℤ[√−5], verify that (2,1+√−5) is a prime ideal: show that ℤ[√−5]/(2,1+√−5)≅𝔽₂. Then show (2,1+√−5)²=(2) (the ideal generated by 2 in ℤ[√−5]).
3. State Minkowski's bound for ℚ(√−5). Use it to show that every ideal class contains an ideal of norm ≤M. List all prime ideals of norm ≤M and explain why they generate Cl(ℚ(√−5))=ℤ/2ℤ.
4. Explain why the Stark-Heegner result (only finitely many imaginary quadratic fields with class number 1) implies that ℤ[√−D] is a UFD for only finitely many values of D. Is ℤ[√−6] a UFD? (h(ℚ(√−6))=2.)

**P55 — Reflect & Consolidate:** "O_K = ring of integers; Dedekind domain; ideal factorisation unique. h_K measures UFD failure. Minkowski bound gives finite computable procedure for h_K. Unit group: Dirichlet theorem. Pell solutions = units of norm 1 in real quadratic O_K."

**P76 — Transfer Probe (Cross-link mode: math.abst.galois-theory):**
(a) For the cyclotomic field K=ℚ(ζ_p) (p prime): the Galois group Gal(K/ℚ)≅(ℤ/pℤ)×. Why is Gal(K/ℚ) abelian? (b) Kummer's approach: if p is an odd prime and p∤h(ℚ(ζ_p)) (p is a 'regular prime'), then Fermat's Last Theorem holds for exponent p (Kummer's theorem). The primes p<100 that are irregular (p|h(ℚ(ζ_p))) are: 37, 59, 67. Explain why h(ℚ(ζ_37))>1 would concern Kummer. (c) Chebotarev Density Theorem: the density of primes that split completely in a degree-n Galois extension is 1/n. For ℚ(√−5)/ℚ (degree 2): half of all primes split completely, a quarter each ramify or remain inert. Verify: 7 is inert (7≡3 mod 4... actually in ℚ(√−5) splitting is determined by Legendre symbol (−5/p)). Compute for p=7: (−5/7)=(−1/7)(5/7)=(−1)^3×(7/5)(−1)^... use quadratic reciprocity.

**P55 — Reflect & Consolidate:** "Cyclotomic fields: Gal(ℚ(ζ_p)/ℚ)≅(ℤ/pℤ)× abelian — this is why abelian extensions of ℚ are all contained in cyclotomic fields (Kronecker-Weber). Class field theory: complete description of abelian extensions in terms of class groups (generalises quadratic reciprocity). Chebotarev: governs prime splitting by Galois group structure."

**P75 — Mastery Assessment:**
"(a) Show that 5 splits in ℤ[i] as (5)=(2+i)(2−i): verify 5=(2+i)(2−i) in ℤ[i], and that 2+i and 2−i are non-associate primes. (b) Compute h(ℚ(i)) using Minkowski's bound. Conclude ℤ[i] is a UFD. (c) In ℚ(√−23): h=3. This means there are ideals that are not principal, but every ideal cubed is principal. Show that the prime 2 is inert in ℤ[(1+√−23)/2] (i.e. (2) remains prime) or splits (use Legendre symbol (−23/2)). (d) Explain in 2-3 sentences why algebraic number theory is needed for Wiles' proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, beyond what Kummer's regular-prime approach already provides."

**P55 — Reflect & Consolidate:** "ℤ[i] is a PID (h=1): every prime p≡1(mod 4) splits as p=(a+bi)(a−bi) (Gaussian prime factorisation); p≡3(mod 4) remains prime. Wiles' proof needs sophisticated machinery beyond Kummer: modularity lifting, Galois representations, deformation theory, Wiles' own ε-conjecture — algebraic number theory at the frontier of modern mathematics."

**P74 — Routing Decision:**
- Score ≥ 3/5 → MASTERED; math.nt.algebraic-number-theory complete
- Score 2/5 → REVIEW ideal factorisation in Dedekind domains and class number; replay A01
- Score ≤ 1/5 → PREREQUISITE GAP in math.abst.ring-theory; reassign

**P78 — Completion:** Algebraic Number Theory certified. Student defines number fields, rings of integers, Dedekind domains; explains UFD failure via class numbers; applies Minkowski's bound; connects to Pell's equation via unit groups; relates to Galois theory; understands Kummer's approach to FLT.
